title: Docker Images, Containers & Basic Commands
description: Learn to manage Docker images and containers with essential docker commands.

data.text: A **Docker image** is a read-only template that contains a snapshot of your application and its environment. Images are built in layers — each layer is a set of filesystem changes. When you run an image, Docker adds a writable layer on top, creating a **container**.

items: Images are **immutable** — you cannot change a running image.
Each image is identified by a **name:tag** (e.g., `nginx:1.25`).
Images consist of multiple **layers** that Docker caches for fast rebuilds.
An image is like a **class** in object-oriented programming; a container is like an **instance**.

data.title: Docker image commands
data.content: List local images, inspect one, and remove an unused image.
data.code:
docker images
docker image ls
docker inspect nginx:latest
docker rmi nginx:1.25

data.text: A **container** is a running instance of an image. It has its own isolated filesystem, network stack, and process space, but shares the host kernel. Containers are ephemeral — when you remove a container, any data written to its writable layer is lost.

rows: Create and start a new container from an image
Run a command inside a running container

data.title: Managing containers
data.content: Run a container, inspect it, and interact with it in real time.
data.code:
docker run -d --name myapp nginx

docker ps
docker inspect myapp
docker logs myapp
docker exec -it myapp /bin/sh
docker stop myapp
docker rm myapp

data.title: Pro tip: run and clean up
data.text: Use `--rm` with `docker run` to automatically remove the container when it stops. This is great for one-off tasks or testing.

terms.definition: A read-only template containing an application and its dependencies. Images are built in layers and identified by name:tag.
A running instance of an image with a writable layer on top. Containers are ephemeral and isolated.
A filesystem change recorded during image build. Layers are cached and reused to make rebuilds fast.
A label applied to an image (e.g., `1.25`, `latest`) that identifies a specific version.
A storage and distribution service for Docker images, such as Docker Hub or a private registry.

data.text: Docker builds images in layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer. When you rebuild an image, Docker reuses unchanged layers from its cache — this is what makes builds fast. But it also means the order of your Dockerfile instructions matters: put rarely-changing instructions at the top and frequently-changing ones at the bottom.

data.caption: Docker images are made of stacked layers. Each layer is a diff of filesystem changes.
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Base Layer: ubuntu:22.04] --> B[+ apt-get update]
    B --> C[+ apt-get install nodejs]
    C --> D[+ Copy app code]
    D --> E[Writable Container Layer]
    style E fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px

items: Install dependencies before copying application code so code changes don't invalidate the dependency layer.
Combine related RUN commands to reduce the number of layers.
Use a small base image (e.g., `alpine`) to reduce image size.
Avoid storing secrets or large temporary files in image layers.

data.title: Practice with Docker commands
data.description: Get hands-on experience with the most common Docker CLI commands.
steps: Pull the official Redis image: `docker pull redis:7-alpine`
Run it in the background: `docker run -d --name redis-test -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine`
Run `docker exec -it redis-test redis-cli ping` to verify Redis responds with PONG.
Clean up: `docker stop redis-test && docker rm redis-test`
data.expectedOutcome: You should see 'PONG' confirming the Redis container is serving requests on port 6379.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Docker images are read-only, layered templates; containers are their running instances.
Use `docker run` with flags like `-d`, `-p`, and `--name` to control container behavior.
Image layers are cached, so ordering Dockerfile instructions for least-churn-at-top maximizes cache hits.
Always clean up stopped containers to save disk space.
data.takeaway: Master the docker CLI fundamentals — images, containers, and layers — before moving on to Dockerfiles.
